# teacher: a small CNN trained on the 505 training images

A 5-block convolutional network (981,802 parameters) trained from scratch on the 505 images in
`workspace/data/train` and nothing else. It is delivered as numpy weights (`cnn_505.npz`, ~3.9 MB)
plus a numpy-only forward pass (`teacher.py`); no torch is needed.

## How it was trained and how it scores
- Recipe (baseline/cnn_small.py, seed 0): AdamW lr 2e-3 wd 0.05, one-cycle schedule, label smoothing 0.1,
  batch 64, 40 epochs, 128 px, random crop from a 144 px resize + flip + brightness/contrast/saturation jitter.
  The final-epoch weights are used (no early stopping or model selection).
- Accuracy: 99.0% on its 505 training images, 68.1% on the 495 validation images, 68.9% on the hidden test set.
  It memorises the training set, so activations on train images look cleaner than they will on unseen images.

## Classes (logit index order)
0 tench, 1 english_springer, 2 cassette_player, 3 chain_saw, 4 church, 5 french_horn, 6 garbage_truck, 7 gas_pump, 8 golf_ball, 9 parachute

## Preprocessing (identical to the training-time eval transform)
RGB; resize shortest side to 144 (PIL bilinear, other side `round(w*s)`); centre crop 128x128;
divide by 255; subtract mean (0.485, 0.456, 0.406) and divide by std (0.229, 0.224, 0.225) per channel; CHW.

## Layers (output shapes for a 128 px input)
| name | operation | output |
|---|---|---|
| conv1 | conv3x3 3->32 (pad 1, no bias) + BN (eps 1e-5) + ReLU | 32x128x128 |
| pool1 | maxpool 2x2 | 32x64x64 |
| conv2 | conv3x3 32->64 + BN + ReLU | 64x64x64 |
| pool2 | maxpool 2x2 | 64x32x32 |
| conv3 | conv3x3 64->128 + BN + ReLU | 128x32x32 |
| pool3 | maxpool 2x2 | 128x16x16 |
| conv4 | conv3x3 128->256 + BN + ReLU | 256x16x16 |
| pool4 | maxpool 2x2 | 256x8x8 |
| conv5 | conv3x3 256->256 + BN + ReLU | 256x8x8 |
| pool5 | maxpool 2x2 | 256x4x4 |
| gap | global average pool | 256 |
| fc | linear 256->10 (logits) | 10 |
| probs | softmax | 10 |

`conv1..conv5` activations are post BN+ReLU. Weights: `features.N.*` (N = index in the 20-layer feature stack:
conv at 0,4,8,12,16; BN at 1,5,9,13,17) and `fc.weight`/`fc.bias`. Full details are in `arch.json`.

## Using it
From `workspace/`:

    import sys; sys.path.insert(0, "teacher"); import teacher
    m = teacher.load()
    m.layers()                                    # [(name, kind, output_shape), ...]
    logits = m.forward("data/train/church/x.JPEG")                 # (10,)
    logits, acts = m.forward(path, return_activations=True)        # acts: ordered dict name -> array
    cls, probs = m.predict(path)
    m.weights("conv2")                            # dict of that layer's parameter arrays

`forward` also accepts an RGB uint8 HxWx3 array (same resize/crop pipeline; pass `already_cropped=True` to skip it).
About 0.15 s per image on CPU.

    python3 teacher/teacher.py layers
    python3 teacher/teacher.py predict IMG [IMG ...]
    python3 teacher/teacher.py activations IMG --layer conv3 [--top-channels 10] [--out maps.npz]
    python3 teacher/teacher.py weights --layer conv1 [--out w.npz]

\"\"\"Analytic colour, texture and geometry evidence; all constants chosen by visual meaning.\"\"\"
import numpy as np
from PIL import Image
import cv2

CLASSES = ('tench','english_springer','cassette_player','chain_saw','church','french_horn','garbage_truck','gas_pump','golf_ball','parachute')


def features(rgb):
    # A 160-pixel square offers enough edges for object structure at a small fixed cost.
    a = cv2.resize(rgb, (160,160), interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA).astype(np.float32)/255
    # RGB and HSV distinguish sky, grass, brass, fur and painted machines.
    r,g,b = a.transpose(2,0,1)
    hsv = cv2.cvtColor(a, cv2.COLOR_RGB2HSV)
    h,s,v = hsv.transpose(2,0,1)
    # Equal-channel brightness avoids making green foliage brighter by convention.
    gray = a.mean(axis=2)
    # These hue intervals represent sky cyan/blue, grass green, warm brass and brown fur.
    masks = dict(blue=(h>175)&(h<260)&(s>.18)&(v>.35), green=(h>65)&(h<170)&(s>.20),
                 gold=(h>28)&(h<65)&(s>.35)&(v>.35), brown=(h>8)&(h<48)&(s>.22)&(v<.65),
                 red=((h<18)|(h>340))&(s>.50)&(v>.35), orange=(h>10)&(h<40)&(s>.55)&(v>.5),
                 white=(s<.20)&(v>.72), black=v<.22, neutral=s<.17,
                 skin=(r>g*1.08)&(g>b*1.10)&(r>.42)&(s<.6))
    f={}
    for k,m in masks.items():
        # Global, central and upper-field proportions separate object from landscape context.
        f[k]=float(m.mean())
        f[k+'c']=float(m[32:128,32:128].mean())
        f[k+'top']=float(m[:60].mean())
        f[k+'bottom']=float(m[100:].mean())
    # Sobel derivatives separate rectilinear machines/buildings from curved organic scenes.
    gx=cv2.Sobel(gray,cv2.CV_32F,1,0,ksize=3)/4
    gy=cv2.Sobel(gray,cv2.CV_32F,0,1,ksize=3)/4
    mag=np.hypot(gx,gy)
    # A contrast difference of about a tenth is an object edge rather than JPEG noise.
    edge=mag>.10
    f['edge']=float(edge.mean())
    # Near-axis gradients indicate horizontal/vertical contours within roughly 15 degrees.
    axis=(np.minimum(abs(gx),abs(gy))<.27*np.maximum(abs(gx),abs(gy)))&edge
    f['axis']=float(axis.sum()/max(edge.sum(),1))
    f['vertical']=float(((abs(gx)>2*abs(gy))&edge).mean())
    f['horizontal']=float(((abs(gy)>2*abs(gx))&edge).mean())
    # Local residual isolates fur, scales, grass and golf dimples from smooth sky and panels.
    residual=gray-cv2.GaussianBlur(gray,(0,0),1)
    f['fine']=float(np.mean(abs(residual)))
    f['smooth']=float((abs(residual)<.015).mean())
    f['contrast']=float(gray.std())
    f['saturation']=float(s.mean())
    # Opposing dark/white patches are common on springer coats, and brown is their fur colour.
    nearwhite=cv2.dilate(masks['white'].astype(np.uint8),np.ones((7,7),np.uint8))>0
    f['brownwhite']=float((nearwhite&masks['brown']).mean())
    f['blackwhite']=float((nearwhite&masks['black']).mean())
    # White object against green lawn is a characteristic golf arrangement.
    f['golfcontext']=f['whitec']*f['green']
    # Sky in upper field with stronger colour low down separates landscapes from airborne canopy scenes.
    f['sky']=f['bluetop']
    return f


def scores(f):
    # Evidence weights below are hand-chosen ordinal votes: strong object clues get several votes,
    # broad context gets one or two; proportions are scaled to make a quarter-image patch meaningful.
    s={k:0.0 for k in CLASSES}
    s['tench']=2*f['skin']+3*f['brownc']+f['green']+2*(1-f['saturation'])-3*f['axis']
    s['english_springer']=8*f['brownwhite']+5*f['blackwhite']+2*f['whitec']+2*f['brownc']+f['green']
    s['cassette_player']=3*f['neutral']+2*f['blackc']+3*f['axis']-2*f['green']-2*f['sky']
    s['chain_saw']=5*f['orange']+3*f['red']+f['green']+f['blackc']+f['edge']
    s['church']=3*f['axis']+2*f['sky']+2*f['vertical']+f['brown']-f['blackc']
    s['french_horn']=7*f['goldc']+3*f['gold']+f['black']-f['green']
    s['garbage_truck']=2*f['axis']+2*f['edge']+f['green']+f['white']+f['red']
    s['gas_pump']=3*f['axis']+2*f['whitec']+2*f['red']+f['blackwhite']-f['green']
    s['golf_ball']=6*f['golfcontext']+2*f['greenc']+2*f['whitec']+2*f['smooth']-f['edge']
    s['parachute']=6*f['blue']+2*f['sky']+f['smooth']-f['axis']
    return s


def predict(path: str) -> str:
    # PIL is the only image reader; RGB conversion makes grayscale and CMYK JPEGs consistent.
    with Image.open(path) as im:
        rgb=np.asarray(im.convert('RGB'))
    # Highest semantic evidence wins; no stored examples or learned parameters are consulted.
    return max(scores(features(rgb)).items(),key=lambda kv:kv[1])[0]

    hsv = cv2.cvtColor(a, cv2.COLOR_RGB2HSV)

    # These hue intervals represent sky cyan/blue, grass green, warm brass and brown fur.

    f={}
    for k,m in masks.items():

        f[k]=float(m.mean())
        f[k+'c']=float(m[32:128,32:128].mean())
        f[k+'top']=float(m[:60].mean())
        f[k+'bottom']=float(m[100:].mean())
    # Sobel derivatives separate rectilinear machines/buildings from curved organic scenes.
    gx=cv2.Sobel(gray,cv2.CV_32F,1,0,ksize=3)/4
    gy=cv2.Sobel(gray,cv2.CV_32F,0,1,ksize=3)/4
    mag=np.hypot(gx,gy)

import cv2
import numpy as np


def geometry_features(rgb):
    # A 128 square gives inexpensive object-scale morphology; the same distortion applies to all classes.
    a = cv2.resize(rgb, (128, 128), interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA)
    # Luminance is the mean of the three primaries, so neutral machinery is not biased to any colour.
    g = a.astype(np.float32).mean(axis=2)
    # Sobel's small derivative detects structural boundaries, while its factor 8 puts gradients in brightness units.
    gx = cv2.Sobel(g, cv2.CV_32F, 1, 0, ksize=3) / 8
    # The perpendicular derivative measures upright facades and equipment sides with the same normalization.
    gy = cv2.Sobel(g, cv2.CV_32F, 0, 1, ksize=3) / 8
    # Ten brightness levels reject JPEG and sensor fluctuations while keeping visible structural edges.
    edge = (np.hypot(gx, gy) > 10).astype(np.uint8)
    # A horizontal edge has a vertical derivative; a 2:1 ratio tolerates perspective without counting roof diagonals.
    he = ((np.abs(gy) > 2 * np.abs(gx)) & (edge > 0)).astype(np.uint8)
    # Vertical edges are similarly isolated for pump posts and church windows.
    ve = ((np.abs(gx) > 2 * np.abs(gy)) & (edge > 0)).astype(np.uint8)
    # Closing gaps of three pixels repairs weak portions of one physical edge without merging whole objects.
    hc = cv2.morphologyEx(he, cv2.MORPH_CLOSE,np.ones((1,3),np.uint8))
    # The transposed kernel repairs upright boundaries.
    vc = cv2.morphologyEx(ve, cv2.MORPH_CLOSE,np.ones((3,1),np.uint8))
    # Twelve pixels is about a tenth of the frame: long enough to indicate structure rather than fur or leaves.
    hl = cv2.morphologyEx(hc,cv2.MORPH_OPEN,np.ones((1,12),np.uint8))
    # The vertical analogue measures walls, window bars, and pump cabinets.
    vl = cv2.morphologyEx(vc,cv2.MORPH_OPEN,np.ones((12,1),np.uint8))
    # Fractions are independent of object resolution; a tiny denominator guard handles entirely flat pictures.
    line = float((hl.sum()+vl.sum()) / (edge.sum()+1))
    # Strong edges meeting the axis criteria are evidence for manufactured objects rather than organic contours.
    axis = float((he.sum()+ve.sum())/(edge.sum()+1))

    panel = g[32:96,32:96]

    dark = g < 85

import numpy as np
import cv2


def round_features(rgb):
    # Work in unit RGB so brightness thresholds express fractions of the display range.
    a = rgb.astype(np.float32) / 255.0
    r, g, b = a.transpose(2, 0, 1)
    # Arithmetic luminance treats all channels alike: no coefficients are learned.
    gray = a.mean(axis=2)
    # Channel spread separates neutral white golf balls from coloured grass and brass.
    spread = a.max(axis=2) - a.min(axis=2)
    # A five-pixel neighbourhood measures small texture without following individual pixels.
    local = cv2.GaussianBlur(gray, (0, 0), 1.0)
    # Fine residual detects golf dimples and brass tube boundaries at this thumbnail scale.
    fine = np.abs(gray - local)
    # Sky blue has more blue than red and is bright; 0.04 allows haze while requiring colour.
    blue = (b > r + 0.04) & (b > g - 0.03) & (b > 0.35)
    # Broad smoothness distinguishes sky from blue lettering, machinery and shaded foliage.
    broad = cv2.GaussianBlur(gray, (0, 0), 3.0)
    # A variation under one twentieth of the range describes a largely smooth sky patch.
    smooth = np.abs(gray - broad) < 0.05

    gold = (r > b + 0.12) & (g > b + 0.06) & (r > g - 0.03) & (g > 0.22)

    white = (gray > 0.55) & (spread < 0.20)

    green = (g > r + 0.03) & (g > b + 0.03)

    f['sky_top'] = float((blue & smooth)[:rgb.shape[0] // 2].mean())

    # Chroma separates colourful housing/vegetation from silver scales and white fur.
    chroma = a.max(axis=2) - a.min(axis=2)
    # A broad centre window discounts corners where background is common; halves and quarters are geometric fractions.
    yy, xx = np.mgrid[0:160, 0:160].astype(np.float32)
    # One half-width gives a smooth, weak centre preference rather than cropping off animals.
    center = np.exp(-((xx / 160 - .5) ** 2 + (yy / 160 - .5) ** 2) / .25)
    # White fur is bright and weakly chromatic; two thirds brightness and one sixth chroma exclude skin.
    white = (v > 2 / 3) & (chroma < 1 / 6)
    # Brown springer patches have ordered RGB, modest saturation and a mid-to-dark value; ratios allow lighting changes.
    brown = (r > g * 1.10) & (g > b * 1.08) & (v > .10) & (v < .60) & (chroma > .06)
    # Black ears or nose share the same coat role as brown patches; one fifth brightness denotes a deep shadow.
    dark = v < .20
    # Nine-pixel neighbourhoods represent neighbouring coat patches rather than pixel noise.
    near_white = cv2.GaussianBlur(white.astype(np.float32), (0, 0), 9)
    # Brown/black patches embedded among white fur are more dog-like than isolated brown soil or black equipment.
    coat_adjacency = float(np.mean((brown | dark) * near_white * center))
    # Olive fish have red and green exceeding blue, with red/green relatively close; chroma excludes gray machines.

    # Fish body mask keeps olive and muted silver-brown while rejecting vivid green foliage and warm dog patches.
    fish_mask = olive & (r > g - .025) & (r < g + .08)
    # A three-pixel opening removes individual grass blades before measuring the body silhouette.
